cards.text: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, is writing a letter to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion. He just told them God chose to give us birth through the word of truth. Now he says, "My beloved brothers, understand this:"

cards.question: James gives his beloved brothers three things to watch. Which one should everyone be QUICK to do?
James also says everyone should be slow to speak and slow to anger.
James gives a reason to be slow to anger. What is it?

answers.text: It doesn't bring about the righteousness God desires
It makes the people around you stop listening
It shows you don't have enough faith in God

cards.text: So James says to get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil. That's scraping the burnt tray, baker, and you don't save a couple black crumbs on there for old times' sake.

cards.question: James gives a second command in that same breath: humbly accept something. What is it?
James says the word planted in them can save their souls.
James says hearing the word isn't enough on its own. What else should his brothers be?
James says if you only hear the word and stop there, you're deceiving ___.

cards.text: Then James paints a picture. Someone who hears the word but doesn't carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror.

cards.question: After the man in the mirror looks himself over, he walks away and remembers exactly what he looks like.

cards.text: And James says he forgets immediately. That's me reading the recipe, turning around to the bowl, and going, "Wait. How many cups of flour?"

cards.question: But James says there's another kind of person, who looks intently into something and keeps at it. What does he look into?

answers.text: The record of his own deeds

cards.question: James says that person, not a forgetful hearer but an effective doer, will be blessed in what he hears.

cards.text: Then James asks us to picture this: what if someone considers himself religious and yet doesn't bridle his tongue? Baker, I've had words leave my mouth so fast my brain had to read about it LATER.

cards.question: That man deceives his heart. And James says his religion is ___.

cards.text: Then James shows what religion that's pure and undefiled before our God and Father looks like. It comes in two parts.

cards.question: James says pure religion means caring for ___ and ___ in their distress.
James says the other part of pure religion is keeping yourself from being polluted by the world.

findings.problem: Too much of the stop depends on luck rather than informed picks. No earlier card gives a basis for the reason in card 4, what must be accepted in card 6, what the attentive person looks into in card 13, or the two groups in card 18. Cards 2, 3, 9 and 19 likewise ask for unrevealed details without enough context to reason them out. Together these make up a majority of the stop's choice cards, beyond the few discovery questions allowed.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer. The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question. A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: The question begins with "That man," but the man is identified only on story card 15, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to identify him as the person who considers himself religious yet does not bridle his tongue.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.
